about: How far each recurring shareholder ask (data/asks.json) is already required by a policy in data/causality.json. full = the policy requires what the ask requests, for the companies asked; partial = it requires part of it, or only in one place or for some companies; none = no listed policy requires it (the note lists what was checked). This site's reading of the policy text, not legal advice. reviewed=false until a person confirms each row.

entries.note: Utah HB 76 makes new large data centers in Utah report annual water withdrawals, published per facility; it does not require region-level water-stress metrics or a human right to water policy.

AB 2619 makes California data centers report expected and prior-year water use to local licensing bodies from 2027; it covers one state and does not require water-stress analysis or public company reports.

Checked the EU AI Act, GPAI Code, DSA, CSDDD, SB 53, the RAISE Act, Colorado SB 26-189, China's AI rules, the UN Guiding Principles, OECD Guidelines and the G7 code; none requires reporting on AI tools sold for oil and gas work.

The EU AI Act makes general-purpose model providers document a model's known or estimated energy use for regulators on request; it requires no public data center emissions, energy or climate-goal reporting.
The EU AI Act requires synthetic content to be machine-marked and deepfakes disclosed from August 2026; it requires no child safety targets, metrics or reports on detection software.
The omnibus adds an EU ban on AI that generates child sexual abuse material or non-consensual intimate images, applying from December 2026; it requires no company child safety reporting.
The voluntary GPAI Code lists child sexual abuse material among risks signatory model providers should consider; it requires no public child safety targets or reports.

The EU AI Act bans AI that manipulates people or exploits vulnerabilities to cause significant harm; it does not require a human rights impact assessment of targeted advertising. This reading is uncertain.

The EU AI Act bans some uses such as untargeted facial image scraping and most live police face recognition in public; it excludes military uses and requires no customer human rights due diligence report.
EU fundamental rights impact assessments for some high-risk AI deployers now start December 2027; they bind deployers, not the vendors investors ask, and exclude military and national security.
The EU AI Act requires AI-generated content to be machine-marked and deepfakes labeled from August 2026; it requires no report on misinformation risks or remediation effectiveness.

Providers of EU systemic-risk models must assess and mitigate systemic risks and report serious incidents to the AI Office; the Act's recitals name disinformation as a possible systemic risk, but its articles require no public misinformation report.

The voluntary GPAI Code names harmful manipulation as a systemic risk and lists a tendency to produce misinformation, and false content, among risk sources to consider; it binds only signatories and requires no public misinformation report.
The EU AI Act requires bias checks on high-risk systems' training data, now delayed to December 2027; it does not cover chatbot viewpoint bias or require a public report.

Colorado SB 26-189 requires notices, explanations and human review for automated decisions in jobs, lending, housing and other consequential areas from 2027, and drops the 2024 act's duty of reasonable care against algorithmic discrimination; it does not cover viewpoint bias or require public reports to investors.
The voluntary GPAI Code lists non-discrimination among risks signatory model providers should consider; it requires no public bias report.
The EU AI Act makes general-purpose model providers publish a training-content summary and keep a copyright policy; it does not require a report on data-misuse risks or how well mitigations work.
The voluntary GPAI Code's copyright chapter commits signatories to respect web crawling opt-outs and handle complaints; it does not cover user data or require a risk report.
Colorado SB 26-189 makes developers give deployers the categories of training data used, to the extent known, from 2027; nothing is published to investors.
The EU AI Act requires employers to inform workers before using high-risk workplace AI, now delayed to December 2027; it does not require a worker AI advisory council.
Colorado SB 26-189 requires notice to people when automated systems materially influence job decisions from 2027; it does not require worker input bodies.

SB 53 makes large frontier developers publish safety frameworks, including internal governance, and model transparency reports; it covers catastrophic risk only and does not require board committee oversight.

The amended RAISE Act makes large frontier developers publish safety frameworks and report incidents, with enforcement delayed until January 2027 (law firm summary); it covers catastrophic risk only, not board oversight.

The EU AI Act makes general-purpose model providers keep documentation for regulators and, for systemic-risk models, assess risks and report incidents; it requires no board oversight or public AI report.

Voluntary: the UN Guiding Principles expect human rights due diligence on impacts linked to a company's products through business relationships, which covers AI customer use; nothing is legally required.
Voluntary: the Guiding Principles' due diligence expectation covers impacts of a company's own operations, including where data centers are built; no law requires it.

Voluntary: the 2023 OECD Guidelines expect technology companies to do due diligence on how their products are used, including by customers; enforcement is limited to National Contact Point complaints.
Voluntary: the 2023 Guidelines expect companies to set and report on emissions targets consistent with the Paris Agreement; they say nothing specific about data centers.
Voluntary: the G7 Code asks advanced AI developers to publish transparency reports and disclose governance and risk policies; it does not mention board oversight.
Voluntary: the G7 Code asks developers to use content authentication and provenance, such as watermarking, where feasible; it requires no misinformation risk report.
Voluntary: the G7 Code asks developers to apply data quality controls and protect personal data and intellectual property; it requires no public data report.

Voluntary: companies that join publish a public report on risk management, transparency and governance; Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, Anthropic, Salesforce, Amazon, Cohere and SoftBank Corp. have filed, others on this site have not.
Voluntary: certification requires top management to set an AI policy, assign roles and run AI risk and impact assessments; nothing is published to investors.
Voluntary: signatories pledged to publish frontier safety frameworks and report on implementation; covers severe risks only, not board oversight.

Voluntary: the New Delhi Frontier AI Impact Commitments ask signers to publish aggregated usage data to inform jobs and skills policy by the next summit; the signer list is not confirmed here and nothing covers worker input.
EO 14110 made developers of large dual-use foundation models report red-team results to Commerce, not the public; revoked January 20, 2025.
NYC employers using automated hiring tools must publish annual independent bias audit summaries; the duty falls on employers in one city, not on AI vendors.
Candidates and employees in NYC must be told when automated hiring tools are used; no worker input body is required.
Illinois employers may not use AI with discriminatory effects in employment decisions from 2026; it covers one state and requires no public bias report.
Illinois employers must notify employees when AI is used for employment decisions; no worker advisory body is required.
Large generative AI providers must offer a free detection tool and embed latent disclosures in AI images, video and audio from August 2, 2026; no misinformation risk report is required.
Generative AI developers must post public training data documentation, including whether it holds personal information, from 2026; it does not require a report on data-misuse risks or user data.
Platforms must remove reported nonconsensual intimate images, including AI deepfakes, within 48 hours from May 2026; no child safety reporting or targets.
Companion chatbot operators must keep self-harm protocols, remind known minors to take breaks and block sexual content for minors from 2026; one state and one product type.
TRAIGA bars AI built with the sole intent of producing child sexual abuse material or deepfakes, or chatbots that impersonate children in sexual chats; no reporting duties.
TRAIGA bars AI developed or deployed with intent to unlawfully discriminate, but disparate impact alone is not enough; no bias testing or reporting.
The FTC's 6(b) orders compel seven companies, including Alphabet, Meta, OpenAI and xAI, to tell the FTC how they test and monitor chatbot harms to minors; answers are not public.
Federal LLM contracts must require ideological neutrality and truth-seeking, which touches viewpoint bias; it applies only to models sold to federal agencies and requires no public report.
Texas makes loads of 75 MW or more pay interconnection study costs and disclose backup generation to the grid operator; it covers grid costs in ERCOT only, not emissions or investor reports.
Oregon puts users of 20 MW or more in their own rate class so data centers bear their grid costs; no emissions or public energy reporting.
Georgia Power may charge new customers above 100 MW their full transmission, distribution and generation costs; it is a utility rule in one state and requires no company disclosure.
Exporters of H200-class chips to China must certify know-your-customer and remote-access safeguards; this is national security screening for one destination, not human rights due diligence.

Very large platforms must assess and reduce systemic risks to minors and publish risk reports and audits, and may not show profiling-based ads to minors; there are no AI-specific child safety targets or metrics.
The guidelines set the benchmark for platforms' Article 28 duty to protect minors, including age assurance and risk reviews; they are not binding and do not require public child safety reports.
UK services children use must assess risks to children and use highly effective age checks for the most harmful content; they need not report AI-specific child safety metrics to investors.

Once commenced, the Act makes supplying tools built to create child sexual abuse images an offence, and it allows illegal content duties to be extended to all AI services; it requires no company reporting.
entries.policy_status: enacted; s.72 not yet in force; no s.248 regulations yet

entries.note: Listed platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, X and YouTube must keep under-16s off accounts in Australia; it does not cover AI products as such or require reports.
AI companion chatbots and generative AI services in Australia must age-check before sexual, violent or self-harm material; no public child safety reporting is required.

Very large platforms and search engines must assess and reduce systemic risks to civic discourse and elections and publish risk reports; this covers their services, not a report on generative AI misinformation as such.
The guidelines expect labels on AI-generated content and red-teaming of generative AI before elections, or equally effective measures; no public misinformation report is required.
Intermediaries in India that enable AI content must label it and embed metadata, and social media intermediaries must get and verify user declarations; no risk report is required.
Korea requires notice of generative AI use and labels on its outputs; it does not require reports on misinformation risks.

The DSA bans, on all online platforms, ads based on profiling with sensitive data and profiling-based ads shown to minors, and requires public ad repositories for very large platforms; it requires no human rights impact assessment of targeted ads.
Under the GDPR as read by the EDPB, training on personal data needs a lawful basis tested case by case and can taint later model use; there is no duty to report publicly on training data.
Meta must offer EU users an objection route and other safeguards before training on their public posts and report to the DPC; the report goes to the regulator, not investors.
Korean high-impact AI operators must run risk management, give explanations and keep human oversight; there is no public bias report duty.

Very large platforms must publish transparency reports, including on automated moderation, explain recommender systems and undergo independent audits; this is not reporting on AI governance generally.
Korea requires risk management, documentation and human oversight for high-impact AI and safety duties for large models; it does not require board oversight disclosures.
The EU AI Act bans emotion recognition at work and requires measures for staff AI literacy; it does not require reporting on AI's effects on workers.

EU data centers of 500 kW or more must report energy use, efficiency, renewable share and waste heat each year to an EU database; per-site data is not published and no company climate goals are required.
Companies in CSRD scope must report scope 1 to 3 emissions and energy use where material, which takes in data centers; it is not data center specific and Omnibus I narrowed who reports.
entries.policy_status: in force; scope narrowed by Omnibus I

entries.note: EU data centers of 500 kW or more must report water input each year to an EU database; there is no public per-site data or water-stress analysis.
Companies in CSRD scope must report water use and impacts if material under the water standard; it is not data center specific.
entries.policy_status: in force; scope narrowed by Omnibus I

entries.note: The largest companies must run human rights due diligence on their own operations and chains of activities from 2029; customer use of products falls outside the CSDDD chain of activities.
Due diligence on adverse human rights and environmental impacts of own operations would cover data center sites of in-scope companies from 2029; it names no siting review.
GB 40879 sets mandatory energy efficiency limits for new and expanded data centers in China; it does not require emissions or cost reporting.
The plan caps PUE for new large data centers in China at 1.25 (1.2 at hubs) through project energy review; it does not require company disclosure of energy, emissions or costs.
PUE, green electricity share and renewable energy plans become review criteria for new computing facilities in China; no public company reporting is required.
Recommendation services must not push minors harmful content or induce addiction and should offer minors' modes; this covers recommendation feeds in China, not child safety reporting.
Generative AI providers must take steps against minors' over-reliance or addiction; there is no duty to assess or report child safety risks.

Large platforms serving minors in China must run regular minors' protection impact assessments, offer a minors' mode and publish a yearly minors' online protection social responsibility report; this is not specific to AI.
AI companion services in China may not offer virtual partner services to minors, need guardian consent under 14 and must offer minors' modes; other AI services are not covered.
Automated pushes and marketing in China must offer a non-personalized option or easy refusal; it does not require a human rights assessment of targeted ads.
Users in China must be able to turn off personalized recommendations and delete profile tags; there is no human rights impact assessment duty.
Deepfake providers in China must label synthetic content and not produce fake news; there is no duty to report on misinformation risks.
Generative AI providers must improve accuracy and reliability, label images and video and act on illegal content; no misinformation risk report is required.

AI services covered by China's algorithm, deep synthesis and generative AI rules must add metadata labels, plus visible labels where content may confuse the public and platforms must flag AI content; it addresses labeling, not assessment or reporting of misinformation risks.

Providers must take effective measures to prevent discrimination by ethnicity, belief, country, region, sex, age, occupation or health in design and training data; no public bias audit or report is required.
Automated decisions using personal data must be transparent and fair with no unreasonable price discrimination; there is no reporting duty.
Recommendation services may not use algorithms for unreasonable price discrimination against consumers; broader bias review or reporting is not required.
Training data must come from lawful sources, respect IP and have consent for personal data, and providers must explain data sources to regulators on request; no public disclosure is required.
Deepfake providers must secure training data, follow personal data rules and get separate consent to edit faces or voices; no public reporting is required.
Generative AI providers must strengthen security management of training data; the rule is general and has no disclosure duty.
AI companion providers must use lawfully sourced training data, guard against data poisoning and assess synthetic data; this covers one service type only.
Platforms that use algorithms to schedule workers must protect pay and rest and refine order allocation, pay and working time rules; this covers platform work in China only.

Providers must set up algorithm review and ethics review systems, publish basic principles of their recommendation algorithms and, for services with public-opinion capacity, file algorithm self-assessment reports with the CAC; filings go to the regulator, not to shareholders.
Generative AI services with public-opinion capacity need security assessments and algorithm filing; these go to regulators and do not require board oversight.
Companies doing AI research in ethically sensitive areas must set up ethics review committees; there is no board-level oversight or public reporting duty.

AI companion providers must submit security assessment reports to provincial regulators at launch, after major changes and on reaching 1 million registered or 100,000 monthly active users; nothing is published to investors.

checks.finding: Framework must cover catastrophic risk thresholds, mitigations, third-party assessment, internal governance; transparency report on model release; no training data, bias, child safety or workforce duties.
Large data centers (75+ acre feet a year) report estimated and annual water withdrawals; per-facility withdrawals published; effective May 6, 2026; new large data centers from July 1, 2026.

checks.finding: Approved September 21, 2026; data centers report expected water use and prior-year annual water use on business license applications. Effective January 1, 2027 per Holland & Knight.

checks.finding: AB 1577 separately requires energy reporting by 10 MW+ data centers to the CEC from 2027; it is not a listed policy event, so not scored.

checks.finding: Art 53(1)(d) public training content summary; Annex XI energy consumption; Art 55 systemic risk duties; Art 50 marking and deepfake disclosure; Art 10, 26(7), 27 high-risk duties.

checks.finding: Specified systemic risks: CBRN, loss of control, cyber offence, harmful manipulation; example risks include misinformation, non-discrimination, CSAM and NCII. Code is voluntary.
Signed May 14, 2026; repeals and reenacts SB 24-205 for automated decision-making technology; developer and deployer duties from January 1, 2027.
xAI suit (joined by DOJ) led to a stipulated order barring enforcement of SB 24-205; whether the stay reaches SB 26-189 is unverified.

Imposes no company disclosure duties; directs litigation and agency actions against state AI laws; carves out child safety and data center infrastructure laws from proposed preemption. Not scored as covering any ask.

checks.finding: Nonbinding federal actions; no company requirements, so not scored.

checks.finding: Govern proposal process or preemption, or are pending/UNVERIFIED; not scored as covering any ask.
